/FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Issued at 255 PM MDT Tue Oct 27 2026

On Friday, we will once again see a broad ridge in place over the 
Central CONUS. This iteration of this familiar weather pattern will 
be less amplified, not supporting warmth as significant as what we 
had earlier this month. With troughing inching into the west coast, 
southwest flow aloft will continue to prevail. Models are in fairly 
good agreement showing low-level south to southeast winds advecting 
in improved low-level moisture to the High Plains Friday while 
moisture aloft improves with another influx of tropical moisture. By 
the end of the day Friday, NAEFS mean precipitable water exceeds the 
90th percentile of climatology for much of the area. As has been our 
problem frequently as of late, we will not have much forcing for 
ascent, despite the abundant moisture. This begins to change Friday 
night as two disturbances are pulled out of the southwest. The first 
will be associated with the remnant moisture of Tropical Storm 
Vance, the latest in the parade of eastern Pacific tropical systems 
pushed into the southwest CONUS. This remnant vort-max will track 
further east than its predecessors, moving mostly over the Plains. 
There is a possibility (about 30% chance) for some showers Friday 
night into Saturday, mainly in the Nebraska panhandle. Another more 
disorganized vort-max tracking further west will bring potential for 
afternoon and evening showers and high elevation snow showers mainly 
to the mountains and adjacent zones on Saturday (Halloween). Other 
than the potential for a few light showers, expect generally good 
trick-or-treat conditions with highs in the mid 50s to mid 60s and 
overnight lows dropping only into the upper 30s to mid 40s. Winds 
look fairly light as well. 

Forecast confidence decreases considerably as we head into the 
Sunday through Tuesday time period. While there is still potential 
for widespread precipitation, the ensemble spread is enormous as a 
very complex weather pattern sets up over the Western CONUS. First, 
a powerful disturbance will race into the southwest, riding on a 
very strong sub-tropical jet stream. Meanwhile, a northern branch 
trough will dive into the northwest and progress eastward 
simultaneously. The northern upper level low may also close off from 
the polar jet itself, adding to the uncertainty. With so many moving 
parts on the board, it is difficult to have much forecast confidence 
in how this will play out. 

In lieu of that, we can discuss some possible scenarios. 
Approximately 45% of LREF members are clustered into a scenario 
showing a more progressive storm system. This is further split 
between about half of this camp showing a storm that remains 
progressive, and half showing a storm that eventually closes off
and strengthens, but this occurs too far east to deliver much 
precipitation to our area. In this scenario, most of the area 
could expect light precipitation amounts, generally 0.25" or 
less. The remaining 55% of ensemble members have a deeper, 
stronger system with better forcing for lift, and thus improving
chances for precipitation. About 30% of the full ensemble suite
(a subset of the 55%) have a moderate precipitation event, 
where the system is strong and deep, but still progressive. The 
final 25% (again a subset of the 55%) depict a slow, strong 
upper level low closing off before reaching our area, which 
would lead to widespread heavy precipitation for much of the 
area, but especially over the High Plains. The ECMWF Extreme 
Forecast Index provides some additional context. EFI values for 
QPF on Monday are only around 0.5 to 0.7, suggesting low 
confidence in a significant event. However, the shift of tails 
values exceed 2.0 over much of the High Plains, which tells us 
that a small subset of ensemble members depict an extreme event.
Thus, the main takeaway at this time should be that at least 
some light precipitation is narrowly favored (60% chance) over 
much of the area Sunday PM into Tuesday AM, and there is 
potential for significant rain and/or snow, but the probability 
of this scenario is fairly low (25% chance) at this time. 
Nonetheless, this is high enough to discuss and continue to 
monitor closely in the coming days. Most model guidance shows 
limited cold air with this system once again, and the wettest 
ensemble members also tend to be the warmest (as these close the
low off faster). This will make snow levels an issue once 
again. Regardless of the precipitation outcome, expect cooler 
temperatures by Monday with blustery conditions. There is 
potential for high winds as well, but we'll wait to get a better
idea of the storm's evolution before diving into those details.
